title: Taming Recent-Data Bias in Time Series Forecasting
one_liner: Stop relying too much on the most recent data points; use a randomized sampling strategy to treat old and new data fairly.
lead: When predicting what comes next in a sequence of numbers (like stock prices or sensor readings), most methods lean too heavily on the newest measurements. If those recent readings are messy or wrong, the forecast falls apart. TameR fixes this by randomly resampling old and new measurements equally, then learns to separate the repeating pattern from the random wobbles in each sample.

problem.h2: The world before: recent data drowns out the rest
paras: When you have a long stream of measurements (stock prices, hourly temperature, server response times), you want a model that can guess the next one. The obvious move is: train on all the old data, but let the recent data matter more, because maybe the pattern changed. Most methods do this by design—they give higher weight to newer rows.

But here is what breaks: if the last few measurements are messy (a sensor glitch, a sudden spike, missing values), the model gets anchored to garbage. It trusts that recent data is always true, so it chases the noise. The forecast becomes unreliable. Even on clean data, this bias means the model is fragile—tiny jitters in recent rows swing the prediction wildly.

callout.html: Forecasting methods trust recent data too much, making them brittle when that data is noisy or wrong.

steps.text: Measure how much the model leans on recent vs. old rows; find the over-reliance.
Instead of using all rows in their time order, randomly pick rows from early, middle, late equally often.
Transform each random sample into a common reference frame so old and new data sit on level ground.
Learn a rule to decompose each sample into repeating cycles and random wobbles.
First learn the split; then train the forecast on the clean pattern part of each sample.

paras: The paper changes which rows the model trains on and how it weights them. Instead of the default pattern (all rows, recent ones matter more), TameR randomly resamples the rows and treats old and new equally. This shifts the model away from chasing recent noise.

hidden.name: Dependence on recent data
paras: This is a measure of how much the model's forecast changes if you tweak the newest few rows. High dependence means the model anchors to recent data; a small jitter at the end swings the output wildly. Low dependence means old and new rows pull equally.

The paper estimates it by checking: if I perturb the last few measurements, how much does the forecast shift? The bigger the shift, the higher the dependence. TameR's randomized sampling strategy keeps this dependence low because it forces the model to learn from all time periods, not just the tail.

heat.caption: Darker means model depends on it more. TameR darkens sample coverage and stability, lightens the corner rows.

reads.html: Dependence-on-recent-data is a number that tells you how brittle the forecast is: if the newest rows change, does the prediction swing a lot? High means brittle, low means stable.

The paper measures how much the model breaks when you add perturbations (noise, missing values, anomalies) to recent data. Low dependence means hard to break: a model that does not lean on recent data will not shatter when recent data is wrong.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the causal chain
paras: The core insight: if you force a model to learn equally from old and new data, it stops overfitting to recent noise. Here is the chain. First, randomized sampling means old rows show up just as often in training as new ones; because the model sees each time period with equal frequency, it cannot build a shortcut that works only on recent data—any shortcut would fail half the time. Second, basis alignment makes sure that when you pull an old sample and a new sample, they are on the same scale, so the learning algorithm does not accidentally treat recent data as a special case. Third, periodicity extraction learns to identify the part of each sample that repeats (the true signal) and the part that bounces around (noise). Because this split is learned on mixed-age samples, the periodic rule works on all time periods, not just recent ones. The two-stage learning then trains the forecast on the periodic parts, which are inherently more stable across time because the repeating pattern changes more slowly than the noise.

Why does this reduce dependence on recent data? Because the forecast is built on the repeating pattern, not the wobbles, and the repeating pattern is the same whether you look at old or new rows. If recent data is noisy, the pattern-extraction module ignores the noise and hands only the true cycle to the forecast. Low dependence follows: the forecast does not swing when recent rows are perturbed.

stages.s: Time series with noise, missing values, anomalies
Randomly resample rows from all time periods equally
Basis alignment: bring each sample to common scale
Periodicity extraction: split each into pattern plus wobble
Two-stage learning: train forecast on pattern only

math.words: For each random sample, decompose it as periodic pattern plus residual noise; train the forecast to predict the pattern; the loss penalizes prediction error on the pattern part and regularizes the split to be smooth.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Sample A (from week 1): raw value 100. Extraction finds pattern=98, noise=2. Forecast predicts 99. Error = (99-98)^2 = 1.0.
Sample B (from week 50): raw value 105. Extraction finds pattern=104, noise=1. Forecast predicts 103. Error = (103-104)^2 = 1.0.
Both samples contribute equally to the loss, even though B is recent. Model learns the pattern, not the bias. Smoothness term = 0.5 (extraction is stable). Total loss = 1.0 + 1.0 + 0.7*0.5 = 2.35.

math.note: The forecast trains only on the periodic part, so it ignores recent noise; randomized sampling forces all time periods to contribute equally to learning.

items.b: The period is hidden or multi-scale.
items.html: If the time series has multiple repeating cycles (daily and weekly patterns overlaid), the extraction module might lock onto only one scale. The forecast then misses the others. Works only when the dominant period is identifiable from samples of all ages.

items.b: Recent data is not just noisy—it is genuinely different.
items.html: If the true pattern actually changed (the system entered a new regime), randomized sampling and periodic extraction will smooth over the change. The model will predict the old pattern, not the new reality. Stability to noise does not mean stability to a real shift in what the system does.

The alignment step transforms samples to a common scale. If the transformation is poorly chosen, it can wash out important scale differences between old and new data. The split module then learns a wrong boundary between pattern and noise.

If the period is stable and the noise is genuinely random (not a regime shift), TameR's strategy of treating all time periods fairly means predictions are equally reliable whether the query is on old or recent rows.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Simulate a time series with a known repeating pattern plus random noise. Add a sudden spike or missing value to the last 5 rows only. Train a baseline model (one that weights recent rows high) and train TameR. On a test set drawn from recent rows, measure forecast error. The baseline's error should jump sharply when you perturb the training data's tail; TameR's error should stay flat. Bonus: measure which models' predictions change most when you replay the same time series with different noise seeds on the tail.
demo.closing: The demo must make it clear that TameR's forecast does not swing when recent rows are noisy, while the baseline's does.
